why: Both moved identical traffic with identical migration diffs, so the decision rests on the system-level work: A turned six separable, live-measured Router levers into validated branches — per-conversation prompt caching, a timeout with real margin, a scoped cheaper model, and the Flex-tier consequence split out as its own business decision — while B built two and parked the rest behind reworks. B is sharper on two specific facts (turn-level economics, and that a fallbacks list actually redistributes healthy traffic at +39%), which dents A's fallback item, but A's set is the one I would rather ship and approve item by item.
A_best: Expert Router leverage, correctly scoped and measured: prompt_cache_key per conversation proven live at -49% on a repeated prefix, and the recognition that a Flex-eligible cheap model silently moves user-waiting traffic to Flex and that a models list disables Flex — surfaced as a separate approve/reject item (i6) rather than buried.
B_best: The economics of a real turn: 13 calls, 90% of input tokens in the retrieval path, 52% of cost in output tokens no Router field can touch — plus building, measuring and withdrawing the fallbacks list after finding Router served 4 of 10 healthy requests from another vendor at +39%, which is the one claim A asserts without testing.
A_worst: Its own counts say 11 of 15 requests are the quantitative agent and 3 the analysis path, yet the cache key lands only on the single chat request; and the -56% model-swap claim comes from one synthesis call, not whole-turn cost, which is exactly the inflation trap B measured at +7% and +219%.
B_worst: Only two branches, and the cheaper of its two levers is set at the wrong scope — one deployment-wide cache key, with per-conversation keying deferred to an invasive Responses port that A demonstrates is three lines on the existing client — while the 60s provider_timeout rests on a wrong 600s client default and leaves no margin under llama-index's own 60s.
